title: Monitor, evaluate and respond to production trends, at

lessons.title: Production indicators in broiler and layer enterprises
lessons.html:
Measuring what matters

A poultry manager cannot manage what is not measured. Production trends show whether a flock is on track long before the financial results arrive. The starting point is a small set of key performance indicators (KPIs) that are calculated the same way every week and compared with the breed standard published by the genetics supplier.

Broiler indicators

  • Liveability: birds alive at the end as a percentage of chicks placed. Track daily and cumulative mortality, and separate first-week mortality, which points to chick quality and brooding.
  • Average live weight and uniformity: weekly sample weighing of a fixed number of birds in several places in the house. Uniformity is the share of birds within a set range of the average.
  • Feed conversion ratio (FCR): kilograms of feed used divided by kilograms of live weight produced. Lower is better.
  • Production efficiency factor: combines liveability, weight, age and FCR into one figure that allows fair comparison between flocks and houses.

Layer and breeder indicators

  • Hen-day production: eggs produced per day as a percentage of hens alive that day.
  • Hen-housed production: eggs per hen originally housed, which also reflects mortality.
  • Egg weight and egg mass: grams of egg per hen per day.
  • Feed per dozen eggs or per kilogram of egg mass.
  • Second-grade eggs: cracks, dirties and floor eggs as a percentage of total.
  • Hatchability and fertility for breeder flocks.

Input indicators

Outputs only make sense next to inputs. Track daily feed and water intake per bird, water-to-feed ratio, house temperatures, lighting hours and body weight against target. A change in an input usually comes before a change in output.

Getting data you can trust

Trends are only as good as the records. Insist on daily recording at fixed times, calibrated scales, a working water meter on every house and feed delivery notes matched to silo readings. Check records weekly and question anything that looks too good or too bad. A spreadsheet or farm system that plots each flock against the breed standard makes trends visible at a glance.

lessons.title: Evaluating trends and taking corrective action
lessons.html:
From numbers to decisions

Monitoring is pointless unless it leads to action. Evaluation means asking three questions every week: Where are we against the standard? Is the gap growing or shrinking? What is causing it?

Reading the trend

Plot each KPI on a graph against flock age, with the breed standard on the same graph. Look for:

  • a sudden step change, such as mortality jumping overnight, which suggests an acute event like disease, a power failure or heat stress;
  • a slow drift away from the standard, such as egg production falling a little each week, which suggests nutrition, lighting, body weight or a chronic health problem;
  • differences between houses on the same farm with the same feed, which point to management or equipment in the weaker house.

Finding the cause

Use a structured approach. List possible causes under headings: chicks or pullets, feed, water, climate and ventilation, lighting, health and vaccination, equipment and people. Check the records for each. Example: a broiler house shows poor FCR and low weights in week three. Water intake dropped two days before feed intake did, and the night temperatures were low because a heater failed. The cause is climate, not feed quality.

Bring in specialists when needed. Your veterinarian should do post-mortems on fresh birds when mortality rises. Your feed company nutritionist can sample feed. Do not change vaccination or medication programmes without veterinary advice, and follow the label and your vet for withdrawal periods.

Responding and following up

  1. Agree a corrective action, who is responsible and by when.
  2. Record the action on the flock record.
  3. Monitor the KPI closely until it returns to the standard.
  4. At depletion, hold a flock review and record lessons for the next placement.

Financially, link KPIs to rand values. A small FCR improvement across a large broiler operation can be worth many thousands of rand per cycle, which helps justify spending on repairs or training.

Key points

  • Compare every KPI against the breed standard and plot it against age.
  • Sudden changes point to acute events; slow drift points to chronic causes.
  • Input changes such as water intake often come before output changes.
  • Use a structured list of causes and involve the vet for health issues.
  • Record corrective actions and review every flock at depletion.
